newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UN Council issues mild rebuke for Cambodia events.
newsitem.headline: UN Council issues mild rebuke for Cambodia events.

text.p: The U.N. Security Council late on Friday broke five days of silence on Cambodia, condemning the violence and urging all parties to settle their differences peacefully.

In a statement read at a public meeting, the 15-member body, however, did not mention the takeover of Second Prime Minister Hun Sen of the coalition government in Phnom Penh or issue any threat of further action.

Most Western diplomats considered the statement unusually mild. Envoys said both China and Japan, for varying reasons, did not want stronger wording in the document, which took several days to negotiate.

Cambodia's unwieldy coalition government collapsed in violence on Saturday when Hun Sen's forces moved against First Prime Minister Norodom Ranariddh's men in the capital. Ranariddh left the country the previous day and came to the United Nations on Thursday to plead his case.
The council called on all parties to respect their commitments under the 1991 Paris peace accords on Cambodia and to hold "free and fair" legislative elections by next year.

"The Security Council is gravely concerned at recent developments in Cambodia, including violence, which have the effect of jeopardising continue progress of the Cambodian peace process, and calls for an immediate end to the fighting," the statement said.

U.N. sources said they did not expect any collective action by the council, whose five permanent members -- the United States, Britain, France, Russia and China -- drew up the Paris accords aimed at ending decades of mass murder, foreign occupation and starvation that devastated Cambodia.

The United Nations then sent 25,000 peacekeepers to Cambodia at a cost of $2 billion to help disarm combatants, enforce human rights and prepare for elections. Many of the provisions in the Paris accords were violated from the start.
The sources also said the council had been cautious in endorsing U.N. political missions, even before the coup, or asking U.N. agencies to cut off aid programmes.
Individually some countries have taken action. The United States said it was suspending its aid for at least 30 days in response to Hun Sen's ouster of Ranariddh.
And the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) said it recognised Ranariddh as co-premier and was delaying Cambodia's entry into its grouping indefinitely.
Japan said it was not cutting off aid but found it difficult to maintain its assistance programme amid fighting.
